comment_text:
A good explanation of what is happening to glaciers in the high Himalaya.  Note that the surge dampens as it gets to larger valleys.  Also note that even though this has happened before no warning system was in place.  This claims that 2 days before the disaster, a debris dam formed which by its nature is unstable.  Why did not anyone see this and tell those down stream about it?
Not mentioned is a third thing about the Himalayas, earthquakes.  An earthquake could trigger a glacier collapse.  
Here is the untold story that none of the news services are talking about.  I asked myself where all this water came from?  A glacier falling into a river would create a big splash but that would become less as it moved downstream.  That would not account for the massive amount of water.  Yes, this mentions a debris dam and that accounts for some of the water.  Then I remembered the flood that inundated Pakistan a few years ago.  That also was not covered fully in the news services.  What happened there was the same as what happened in Nepal.  A big monsoon dumped a lot of rain into the mountains.  The hydroelectric dams were full, getting ready for the winter irrigation of crops.  The water surged over the tops of those dams collapsing them like dominos.  By the time the water left the mountains and hit the lowlands it was a huge wall of water.  The Nepalis also had dams on that river and they collapsed when that surge hit the highest dam.  That dam collapsed sending an even bigger surge to the next, and so on.  In other words this was a man made disaster.  It was also preventable since they knew about the disastrous Pakistani flood of October 2022.  
Yes, it is a tragedy, and it has caused a lot of misery to a people who were struggling to get by.  I feel bad for them, and hope they take action to get a warning system.  A simple system like a watchman with a cell phone or portable shortwave radio would be enough.  Yes, someone would have to do the night duty since this can happen at any time.

Pretty crazy looking back through history. Major recorded tsunamis and massive waves caused by earthquakes, volcanoes and landslides appear to have gone from being hundreds of years apart to decades apart, and now sometimes only years apart.

To simplify it into three parts:

Historical accounts (hundreds to thousands of years ago): Major recorded events could appear around 100–250+ years apart, sometimes even longer.

Brief past (roughly the last 100 years): Major recorded events were often around 15–30 years apart or less.

Modern times: Major recorded events can appear around 5–10 years apart or less, with some of the tsunami events we tracked only 1–7 years apart.

Could it just be because we have much better recording, tracking and detection technology today, while historical records are far less complete. But looking at the recorded timeline, the pattern is definitely interesting.
Now there are two theories to take into account.

Firstly, we have so much advanced technology that tracking every major critical event is now better than ever. We can see everything happening in real time and so on with all this new tracking technology.

Secondly, it's basically us humans. With all the modernisation and progress of civilisation after the Industrial Era, human technological advancement has skyrocketed. At the same time, the Earth's temperature has been rising, which could increase the likelihood of events like this. This could also indicate why we've seen other major landslides this year alone, including in Switzerland and India, etc.

It's still crazy how we went from natural disasters not happening as much to now, where it's almost like a daily thing and people don't seem to understand the tracking statistics of these events and what these could imply.

comment_text:
As of yesterday, Friday, 18 September 2026, there are over 1,600 confirmed dead and more than 6,000 missing. These numbers will change as infrastructure and communications with affected areas are reestablished in the coming weeks and months.

The mountain had indications of potential trouble weeks before the disaster, but no one took heed. The incident started as a rock & ice avalanche, with an initial estimated volume of approximately 200M cu. m. (262M cu. yds.). It fell several thousand feet into the valley below, sloshed up the other side briefly, chewed up more ice, then ran down the valley to the river below, chewing up a buried tongue of ice as it went. The ice quickly melted due to frictional heating, which made the mass more fluid. What started as an avalanche quickly became a debris flow. That's what wiped the border crossing off the map, killing nearly everyone in the CCTV clip. From there, it evolved into a mud flow as larger debris was deposited and left behind, then transformed into a flash flood of mostly water and fine sediment, finally petering out in northern India, more than 80 km (50 mi.) downstream.

Due to the nature of the initial event, searchers are finding body parts rather than whole bodies, and some victims will never be found, except as fossils millions of years from now.

comment_text: Langtang? I took that trek back in 1971 with 3 Americans - Ken, Diana & Jeff from Lansing, Mich - 90 miles or 10 day's hike  from the bus drop off point to the Cheese Factory (built by the Swiss in the '50s to process Yak milk) right below Langtang peak. We stayed at their window-less guest house where starting a fire was a struggle, even using the traditional 3 stone method. The spot was what can only be described as awesome, like reaching the end of the earth. Behind the Cheese Factory was a mount whose steep, grassy, southern slope took one to around 12-13k feet. The N side was snow covered. We must have spent 6/hrs up there on the top awed by the solitude, majesty & grandeur of what we could see. To the right of the 23k+feet Langtang peak were 3 separate glaciers emptying into the basin below - like a giant amphitheatre. We watched & listened to almost constant cracks & thunderous roars as huge pieces of ice broke off & fell into this basin. To the right was a Tibetan icefield & Shishmapangma in the far distance, just a sea of white stretching forever. We were trying to spot a team of Japanese climbers ascending Langtang peak but never saw them. We had to make a quick descent before 4pm as clouds would come barreling up Langtang valley. They were so dense they'd obliterate our view of everything so it was easy to lose orientation & fall. It was very steep so if one fell, one would either slide or roll 1000' to the nearest flat ground by the factory or another 2000' on the full southern slope. I remember the Langtang hike as offering an incredible variety of beautiful views, snowy peaks, woods, vegetation, glacial streams & rivers. The trek was physically exhausting but also exhilarating. The Nepalese (& many Tibetan refugees) were hospitable & friendly. At the time there was not one hotel, restaurant or eatery on this trail. Above 9kfeet you carried your own food (potatoes, eggs, cheese.) "Chai" houses offered very sweet green tea about every 5 to 10 miles. We carried cigarettes & candy to give to the many little children who crowded us at every village (they were always a pleasure, and yes, 10/yr. olds accepted cigarettes & - I think - smoked them.) We slept & were fed at any one of the villager's huts who wanted to put us up - it was a source of income for them & quite a unique experience for us - we didn't speak their lingo nor they ours. One couldn't help but love & appreciate these lovely, hardy people. They were poor in goods but rich in what matters. I know that in the 55/yrs. since we were there much has changed. The country has prospered somewhat, Tibet is no longer called that & hotels, eateries & other businesses have sprung up on the lovely Himalayan trails & western & Chinese influence has crept into their society but I'll always love the people & the place. The Langtang area has suffered greatly, what with the massive landslide around 10/yrs. ago that wiped out the village & killed hundreds to now, this terrifying landslide & flood. I pray for you, Nepal.

Even if the monitoring devices were built to warn about floods, the fact that they went offline sequentially is a huge data point. That sequential failure alone should have been a red flag that something was going horribly wrong, and it might have been enough to issue an early warning. There are always other ways to get alerts, and I'm sure redundant systems will be put in place now. Unfortunately, it is already too late for those who lost their lives. This fits a tragic, historical pattern. As a species, we rarely implement the perfect solution for a disaster that has not happened yet because we learn almost entirely from hindsight. While foreseeing every anomaly is technically possible, it is rarely deemed economically justifiable until it is too late. It is hard to blame the original engineers for an incredibly improbable event when the system was first built. However, with global warming accelerating, these improbable events are becoming frequent and violent. We are looking at a grander, systemic shift. The massive rock-and-ice collapse that obliterated valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border is the extreme end of the spectrum, but the underlying trigger is exactly the same as much less violent, localized anomalies. We see this with the tragic avalanche on Broad Peak that took out Nirmal Purja and his team. Rising temperatures are thawing permafrost and destabilizing mountain bedrock everywhere.
